items.stem: Define a force.
items.answer: A push or a pull on an object
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A force – a push or a pull on an object.

items.stem: If equal forces act on a box from opposite sides, the box:
items.answer: does not move
items.markingKey: (a) does not move.

items.stem: A football lying on the ground does not move by itself. Why does it start moving when kicked?
items.answer: An unbalanced force (the kick) acts on it and changes its state from rest to motion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: unbalanced force. 1 mark: changes state of motion.

items.stem: In a tug of war, Varun pulls with 58 N and Ishaan pulls with 35 N in the opposite direction. Find the net force and its direction.
items.answer: 23 N towards Varun
items.markingKey: Opposite directions: subtract, 58 − 35 = 23 N, in the direction of the larger force (Varun).

items.stem: Tara and Aditi push a heavy almirah in the same direction with forces of 25 N and 59 N. What is the net force on it?
items.markingKey: Same direction: forces add, 25 + 59 = 84 N.

items.stem: Sort these by the effect of force they show — a change in shape or a change in speed: (1) applying brakes to a scooter; (2) squeezing a sponge; (3) kicking a football lying at rest; (4) kneading clay into a pot.
items.answer: A change in shape: kneading clay into a pot; squeezing a sponge. A change in speed: applying brakes to a scooter; kicking a football lying at rest.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): A change in shape: kneading clay into a pot; squeezing a sponge. A change in speed: applying brakes to a scooter; kicking a football lying at rest.

items.stem:
Read: Siddharth's cycle squeaks and is hard to pedal. His father oils the chain and axle. On a rainy day the brakes are less effective and Siddharth skids at a turn.
(i) Why does oiling make pedalling easier? (ii) Why do brakes work less well when wet? (iii) Which feature of the tyres helps prevent skidding? (iv) Give one disadvantage of friction in a cycle.
items.answer: (i) Oil reduces friction between moving parts. (ii) Water forms a thin layer that reduces friction between brake pads and rim. (iii) Treads on tyres. (iv) Wear and tear of tyres/brake pads; energy lost as heat.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: A goalkeeper catches a fast football. Name all the effects of the force applied by the goalkeeper on the ball.
items.answer: The ball slows down and stops (change in speed); its direction changes if deflected; it is squeezed slightly (change in shape).
items.markingKey: 1 mark per effect (max 3).

items.stem: Distinguish between mass and weight (any three points). A girl of mass 45 kg goes to the Moon. Find her weight on the Earth and on the Moon (g = 9.8 m/s², Moon's gravity one-sixth).
items.answer: Mass: quantity of matter, kg, same everywhere, measured by a beam balance. Weight: pull of gravity, newton, changes with place, measured by a spring balance. Earth: 45 × 9.8 = 441 N; Moon: 441 ÷ 6 = 73.5 N.
items.markingKey: 3 marks: differences; 2 marks: calculations.

items.stem: Which of the following shows that a force can cause a change in shape?
items.answer: pressing a ball of dough into a roti
items.markingKey: (c) Pressing a ball of dough into a roti is a change in shape. The others: a goalkeeper deflecting a ball – a change in direction; a batsman hitting a ball towards the boundary – a change in direction; applying brakes to a scooter – a change in speed.
options: a batsman hitting a ball towards the boundary
pressing a ball of dough into a roti

items.stem: A force always acts:
items.answer: when objects interact with each other
items.markingKey: (b) when objects interact with each other.
options: when objects interact with each other

items.stem: Rolling friction is ______ sliding friction.
items.answer: smaller than
items.markingKey: (c) smaller than.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A ball rolling on grass stops sooner than one rolling on a cement floor.
Reason (R): Grass offers more friction than a smooth cement floor.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Why do we need a larger push to start moving a heavy box than to keep it moving?
items.answer: Static friction is larger than sliding friction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: static > sliding. 1 mark: application.

items.stem: Diya rolled the same marble down the same ramp onto different surfaces and measured how far it travelled: a glass sheet – 140 cm; a polished marble floor – 125 cm; a jute mat – 50 cm. Which surface has the most friction and which the least? Give a reason.
items.answer: Most friction: a jute mat; least: a glass sheet.
items.markingKey: The marble stops soonest where friction is largest (a jute mat) and travels farthest where it is smallest (a glass sheet). 1 mark each + 1 mark reason.

items.stem: Rahul rolled the same marble down the same ramp onto different surfaces and measured how far it travelled: sand – 30 cm; a newspaper – 95 cm; a jute mat – 50 cm. Which surface has the most friction and which the least? Give a reason.
items.answer: Most friction: sand; least: a newspaper.
items.markingKey: The marble stops soonest where friction is largest (sand) and travels farthest where it is smallest (a newspaper). 1 mark each + 1 mark reason.

items.stem: Explain why it is difficult to write on a glass surface with a pen but easy to write on paper.
items.answer: Writing needs friction between the nib and the surface; paper is rough and gives friction, glass is very smooth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: friction needed. 1 mark: glass smooth.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The force produced by the action of muscles in our body or in animals."
items.answer: muscular force
items.markingKey: (c) Muscular force is the force produced by the action of muscles in our body or in animals.

items.stem: Define a non-contact force.
items.answer: A force that acts on an object without being in contact with it
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A non-contact force – a force that acts on an object without being in contact with it.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of a contact force?
items.answer: friction between tyres and road
items.markingKey: (c) Friction between tyres and road is a contact force. The others: a mango falling from a tree – a non-contact force; a comb after combing dry hair attracting hair – a non-contact force; the Moon being pulled by the Earth – a non-contact force.
options: a mango falling from a tree
the Moon being pulled by the Earth
a comb after combing dry hair attracting hair

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Electrostatic force acts only between objects in contact.
Reason (R): A charged comb can attract bits of paper from a distance.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A false; R true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of a non-contact force?
items.answer: a horse pulling a tonga
items.markingKey: (a) A horse pulling a tonga is a contact force, not a non-contact force. Each of the others (a magnet pulling an iron pin from a distance, a mango falling from a tree, the Moon being pulled by the Earth) is a non-contact force.
options: a mango falling from a tree
a magnet pulling an iron pin from a distance
the Moon being pulled by the Earth

items.stem: Classify these as a non-contact force or a contact force: (1) friction between tyres and road; (2) the push of a hand opening a door; (3) a comb after combing dry hair attracting hair; (4) a magnet pulling an iron pin from a distance.
items.answer: A non-contact force: a comb after combing dry hair attracting hair; a magnet pulling an iron pin from a distance. A contact force: friction between tyres and road; the push of a hand opening a door.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): A non-contact force: a comb after combing dry hair attracting hair; a magnet pulling an iron pin from a distance. A contact force: friction between tyres and road; the push of a hand opening a door.

items.stem: A floating ring magnet stays above another ring magnet on a pencil. Name the forces acting on it and explain why it floats.
items.answer: Gravity pulls it down; magnetic repulsion from the lower magnet (like poles facing) pushes it up; these balance, so it floats.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: forces named. 1 mark: balance explained.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of a non-contact force?
items.answer: the Moon being pulled by the Earth
items.markingKey: (b) The Moon being pulled by the Earth is a non-contact force. The others: a horse pulling a tonga – a contact force; the push of a hand opening a door – a contact force; the force of a hammer on a nail – a contact force.
options: the push of a hand opening a door
the Moon being pulled by the Earth
the force of a hammer on a nail

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of a non-contact force?
items.answer: a racket hitting a shuttlecock
items.markingKey: (d) A racket hitting a shuttlecock is a contact force, not a non-contact force. Each of the others (a comb after combing dry hair attracting hair, a mango falling from a tree, a magnet pulling an iron pin from a distance) is a non-contact force.
options: a magnet pulling an iron pin from a distance
a mango falling from a tree
a comb after combing dry hair attracting hair

items.stem: What is meant by a spring balance?
items.answer: A device that measures force (such as weight) by the stretching of a spring
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A spring balance – a device that measures force (such as weight) by the stretching of a spring.

items.stem: What is the weight of a 45 kg bag of rice on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
items.markingKey: (b) Weight = mass × g = 45 × 9.8 = 441 N.

items.stem: Why would a spring balance show a smaller reading on the Moon for the same object?
items.answer: The Moon's gravity is weaker (about one-sixth), so it pulls the object with less force.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weaker gravity. 1 mark: smaller weight.

items.stem: What is the weight of a 10 kg bag of rice on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
items.markingKey: Weight = mass × g = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.

items.stem: Farhan has a mass of 36 kg. Find Farhan's weight on the Earth and on the Moon (g = 9.8 m/s²; gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth). What is the mass on the Moon?
items.answer: Earth: 352.8 N; Moon: about 58.8 N; mass stays 36 kg.
items.markingKey: W = 36 × 9.8 = 352.8 N; on Moon 352.8 ÷ 6 ≈ 58.8 N; mass does not change.

items.stem: Rohan has a mass of 36 kg. Find Rohan's weight on the Earth and on the Moon (g = 9.8 m/s²; gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth). What is the mass on the Moon?
items.answer: Earth: 352.8 N; Moon: about 58.8 N; mass stays 36 kg.
items.markingKey: W = 36 × 9.8 = 352.8 N; on Moon 352.8 ÷ 6 ≈ 58.8 N; mass does not change.

items.stem:
Read: Priya hung different weights on a spring balance and noted the stretch of the spring: 1 N – 1 cm; 2 N – 2 cm; 3 N – 3 cm; 4 N – 4 cm.
(i) How much does the spring stretch for each newton? (ii) What stretch would a 6 N weight produce? (iii) A packet of mass 0.8 kg is hung from it. Find its weight (g = 9.8 m/s²) and the stretch. (iv) Would the stretch be more, less or the same on the Moon? Why?
items.answer: (i) 1 cm per N. (ii) 6 cm. (iii) 7.84 N; about 7.8 cm. (iv) Less, because the Moon pulls the packet with about one-sixth of the force.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: What is the weight of a 20 kg bag of rice on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
items.markingKey: Weight = mass × g = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N.

items.stem: What is the weight of a 25 kg bag of rice on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
items.markingKey: Weight = mass × g = 25 × 9.8 = 245 N.

items.stem: A spring balance stretches 40 cm when an object of weight 8 N hangs from it. How much will it stretch for an object of weight 24 N (assume the stretch is proportional to the force)?
items.answer: 120 cm
items.markingKey: Stretch per newton = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 cm/N; 24 × 5 = 120 cm.

items.stem: What is the weight of a 12 kg bag of rice on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
items.markingKey: Weight = mass × g = 12 × 9.8 = 117.6 N.

items.stem: What is meant by drag?
items.answer: The frictional force exerted by a fluid such as air or water on an object moving through it
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Drag – the frictional force exerted by a fluid such as air or water on an object moving through it.

items.stem: Which of the following is a way of reducing friction?
items.answer: putting wheels under a suitcase
items.markingKey: (a) Putting wheels under a suitcase is a way of reducing friction. The others: grooves on shoe soles – a way of increasing friction; sprinkling sand on a slippery path – a way of increasing friction; spikes on sports shoes – a way of increasing friction.
options: sprinkling sand on a slippery path

items.stem: Why do we rub our hands together on a cold day?
items.answer: Friction between the palms produces heat that warms them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: friction. 1 mark: heat.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a way of reducing friction?
items.answer: grooves on shoe soles
items.markingKey: (c) Grooves on shoe soles is a way of increasing friction, not a way of reducing friction. Each of the others (oiling a squeaky door hinge, putting wheels under a suitcase, using ball bearings in a cycle wheel) is a way of reducing friction.
options: using ball bearings in a cycle wheel

items.stem: Sort these into a way of increasing friction and a way of reducing friction: (1) spikes on sports shoes; (2) treads on tyres; (3) using ball bearings in a cycle wheel; (4) the streamlined shape of a boat; (5) gymnasts applying powder to their hands.
items.answer: A way of increasing friction: gymnasts applying powder to their hands; spikes on sports shoes; treads on tyres. A way of reducing friction: the streamlined shape of a boat; using ball bearings in a cycle wheel.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): A way of increasing friction: gymnasts applying powder to their hands; spikes on sports shoes; treads on tyres. A way of reducing friction: the streamlined shape of a boat; using ball bearings in a cycle wheel.

items.stem: Vihaan rolled the same marble down the same ramp onto different surfaces and measured how far it travelled: a cotton towel – 60 cm; a jute mat – 50 cm; a glass sheet – 140 cm. Which surface has the most friction and which the least? Give a reason.
items.answer: Most friction: a jute mat; least: a glass sheet.
items.markingKey: The marble stops soonest where friction is largest (a jute mat) and travels farthest where it is smallest (a glass sheet). 1 mark each + 1 mark reason.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a way of increasing friction?
items.answer: the streamlined shape of a boat
items.markingKey: (b) The streamlined shape of a boat is a way of reducing friction, not a way of increasing friction. Each of the others (treads on tyres, sprinkling sand on a slippery path, spikes on sports shoes) is a way of increasing friction.
options: the streamlined shape of a boat
sprinkling sand on a slippery path

items.stem:
Read: A shopkeeper finds it hard to push a heavy carton of books across the floor. When he puts it on a trolley with wheels, he can move it easily. Later he sprinkles talcum powder on a carrom board.
(i) Which type of friction acts when the carton is pushed on the floor? (ii) Why is the trolley easier? (iii) What does the powder do? (iv) Name one force other than friction acting on the carton.
items.answer: (i) Sliding friction (static at the start). (ii) Rolling friction is much less than sliding friction. (iii) Reduces friction so the striker and coins slide easily. (iv) Gravity (weight) or the push of the floor/muscular force.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Harpreet rolled the same marble down the same ramp onto different surfaces and measured how far it travelled: a newspaper – 95 cm; sand – 30 cm; a cotton towel – 60 cm. Which surface has the most friction and which the least? Give a reason.
items.answer: Most friction: sand; least: a newspaper.
items.markingKey: The marble stops soonest where friction is largest (sand) and travels farthest where it is smallest (a newspaper). 1 mark each + 1 mark reason.

items.stem: In a tug of war, Ananya pulls with 66 N and Harleen pulls with 71 N in the opposite direction. Find the net force and its direction.
items.answer: 5 N towards Harleen
items.markingKey: Opposite directions: subtract, 71 − 66 = 5 N, in the direction of the larger force (Harleen).

items.stem: Why does a mango fall downwards and not upwards when it breaks from the tree?
items.answer: The Earth pulls everything towards its centre by gravitational force.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: gravity. 1 mark: towards the Earth's centre.

items.stem:

(i) How much does the spring stretch for each newton? (ii) What stretch would a 6 N weight produce? (iii) A packet of mass 0.8 kg is hung from it. Find its weight (g = 9.8 m/s²) and the stretch. (iv) Would the stretch be more, less or the same on the Moon? Why?
items.answer: (i) 1.5 cm per N. (ii) 9 cm. (iii) 7.84 N; about 11.8 cm. (iv) Less, because the Moon pulls the packet with about one-sixth of the force.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

options: a comb after combing dry hair attracting hair
a magnet pulling an iron pin from a distance

gymnasts applying powder to their hands

items.stem: Which term is described here? "Forces on an object that cancel each other so that its state of motion does not change."
items.answer: balanced forces

items.answer: The force that opposes the motion of one surface over another surface in contact
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Friction – the force that opposes the motion of one surface over another surface in contact.

items.stem: Varun rolled the same marble down the same ramp onto different surfaces and measured how far it travelled: a glass sheet – 140 cm; sand – 30 cm; a jute mat – 50 cm. Which surface has the most friction and which the least? Give a reason.
items.answer: Most friction: sand; least: a glass sheet.
items.markingKey: The marble stops soonest where friction is largest (sand) and travels farthest where it is smallest (a glass sheet). 1 mark each + 1 mark reason.

items.stem: What is the weight of a 2.5 kg bag of rice on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
items.markingKey: (a) Weight = mass × g = 2.5 × 9.8 = 24.5 N.

items.stem: What is the weight of a 4 kg bag of rice on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
items.markingKey: Weight = mass × g = 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): In a tug of war, if both teams pull equally hard, the rope does not move.
Reason (R): Equal and opposite forces on an object are balanced and the net force is zero.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: In a tug of war, Aarav pulls with 55 N and Tanvi pulls with 89 N in the opposite direction. Find the net force and its direction.
items.answer: 34 N towards Tanvi
items.markingKey: Opposite directions: subtract, 89 − 55 = 34 N, in the direction of the larger force (Tanvi).

items.stem: Three boys push a cart: two push forward with 40 N each and one pushes backward with 50 N. Will the cart move? Explain with the net force.
items.answer: Net force = 40 + 40 − 50 = 30 N forward; it is unbalanced, so the cart starts moving forward.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: calculation. 1 mark: direction and conclusion.
